messages:
eva: Heads-up — ran a new sweep on continuous-batching + stream flush cadence this morning. Wanted to share profiling and an unexpected perf/regression pattern I found.

sam: Nice, summary?

eva: TL;DR: changing flush cadence from 12ms -> 8ms reduced tail latency for short chat requests but increased overall GPU kernel switches. That + our kernel-selection fallback causes a perf bump for mid-length requests (~512 tokens).

eva: We tested three dims: flush cadence, token-budget threshold (per-queue moving avg), and KV prefetch window. Each experiment ran 10k requests with mixed user lengths.

ben: Can you paste the key perf numbers?

eva: Sure — median p50/p95/p99 for short (<=64 toks): baseline(12ms) = 22/48/120ms -> 8ms cadence = 18/40/105ms. For mid (128-512): baseline = 60/180/420ms -> 8ms = 72/210/530ms (ouch).

eva: GPU utilization increased 6pp on average in 8ms runs, and we saw kernel change count increase ~1.7x per request for mid-length traffic.

anita: That's consistent with kernel churn — smaller flush windows fragment batches more, so kernel selector sees more heterogeneous sequence-length distributions. Selector then sometimes picks a different attention kernel which restarts some buffers.

perf-bot: PROFILE_SUMMARY: run_id=2026-03-17-08:23, cadence=8ms, token_budget=16, kv_prefetch=48 -> avg_kernel_switches=2.1, mean_gpu_ms_per_token=0.42

sam: Did you try increasing the token_budget target to counter fragmentation?

eva: Yep. Increasing token_budget from 16->24 brought mid-length p95 down from 210ms -> 185ms, p99 from 530->460ms, but short p50 regressed slightly (18->20ms). So it's a tradeoff.

kevin: What about KV cache behavior? Prefetch window change?

eva: Lowering KV prefetch (from 64 to 32) reduced memory pressure and slightly improved kernel selection stability (fewer forced quantized kernels due to memory fallback). But too low and we hurt long-form reuse.

ben: Any specifics on the kernel selector heuristics? Which feature flips it?

eva: The selector currently thresholds on two signals: 1) effective_max_seq_in_batch (RMS) 2) memory headroom estimate. With flush cadence tighter, RMS drops but variance increases. The variance pushes selector to pick the more conservative kernel optimized for higher seq variance, which is slower per-token for medium seqs.

anita: Could we run a lightweight variance-aware smoothing to the RMS estimate? Like exponential moving average over 50 batches before switching kernels? Might reduce flip-flop latency.

eva: I tried EMA with alpha=0.08 — it reduced kernel switches by ~30% and improved mid p95 by ~15ms. But it delayed beneficial switches sometimes, so long-tail for corner cases got worse.

perf-bot: REGRESSION_ALERT: experiment 1900123456-batch-sweep -> mid-length p99 crossed baseline by +22%.

sam: For streaming UX, lower tail for short requests is high priority. Customers running chat care more about p95 for <64. Can we do a hybrid policy: aggressive flush cadence for queues dominated by short sequences, conservative otherwise?

eva: We already have per-queue policy hooks. The new idea: add a lightweight classifier on the queue (sliding histogram of recent seq-lengths) and set cadence & token_budget per-queue dynamically. Prototype config: if >70% short, cadence=6ms token_budget=12; elif mix then cadence=10ms token_budget=22; else cadence=14ms token_budget=28.

ben: Sounds promising. Any prototype numbers?

eva: Simulated routing with per-queue dynamic policy improved overall weighted p95 by ~8% vs fixed 8ms, and mid-length regressions disappeared. Kernel switches normalized.

anita: How stable is the histogram classifier under bursty traffic? Could flip on transient spikes and thrash policies.

eva: We add hysteresis (must meet threshold for 30s) and a cool-down of 45s post-change. That cut policy thrash in sim.

kevin: For partial-decode scheduling — any changes to priority queue ordering? Earlier partial decode starvation issues?

eva: We moved to a two-tier decode queue: fast-path for already-prefetched KV + short partial tokens, slow-path for long-blocking decodes. This reduced partial-starvation by ~40%. Also limited preemption to only when estimated remaining decode > 256 tokens.

sam: Next steps?

eva: 1) Roll out per-queue dynamic cadence prototype to a canary fleet (small % of production). 2) Add variance-smoothing to kernel selector with configurable alpha. 3) Keep KV prefetch default at 48 but make it tunable per-queue. 4) Monitor perf-bot alerts on mid-p99 for 48h.

ben: Agreed. Please capture the experiment config and scripts in the perf repo.

eva: Will do. Pasted the quick run command here:

```
./perf/run_sweep --cadences 6,8,10,14 --token_budgets 12,16,22,28 --kv_windows 32,48,64 --duration 10000
```

kevin: Thanks — if canary looks good we can flip on for chat tier. :thumbsup:

anita: One ask: add a trace tag that logs kernel_id + rms_variance per-batch so we can correlate when we see regressions in the wild.

eva: Yep adding that to the tracer now. I'll post the canary run id and a short dashboard link once live.

perf-bot: NOTE: next scheduled report in 4h.
